As of 124 PM EST Monday...

KEY MESSAGE 1: Multi layer stacked low pressure currently rotating over 
far eastern Quebec, centered near Anticosti Island, will keep our 
forecast area in classic dreary November weather into the late week. 
Clouds continue to blanket northern New York and Vermont this 
afternoon and tonight with scattered to isolated showers, then our 
next shortwave comes through Tuesday, greatly increasing 
probabilities of precipitation Tuesday and Tuesday night. Daytime 
highs in the mid 40s to mid 50s will mean this precipitation mainly 
falls in the form of rain during daylight hours. The cold pool aloft 
and some meager instability could allow for more robust showers to 
produce some graupel on Tuesday afternoon, along with brief 
moderately heavy rainfall and gusty winds. Overall winds out of the 
southwest will be breezy Tuesday, particularly on summits and 
eastern slopes of mountains. Gusts to 30 mph will be possible on the 
eastern slopes, with 35 to 45+ mph atop the mountain summits. A 
reinforcing shot of cold air Tuesday night will bring snow levels as 
low as 1500 ft or so, mainly along the international border and the 
northern Adirondacks/Greens, and this is the best chance for seeing 
any accumulating snow below 2000 ft, though even then, it'll be 
pretty minimal. Lows by Wednesday morning will fall into the mid 20s 
to mid 30s. During the day Wednesday, we'll be drying out under high 
pressure, with perhaps a lingering shower or two in morning for the 
Northeast Kingdom and seasonable afternoon highs in the 40s and 
lower 50s. Total precipitation amounts Tuesday through Wednesday 
will be as high as 0.10-0.30", with highest in the northern 
mountains and Northeast Kingdom. Total snow accumulations will 
likely be under an inch, limited to highest elevations.

KEY MESSAGE 2: There remains high uncertainty with the late week 
system, but trends have continued to suggest a track shift south and 
east of the region with the newest round of guidance. A broad closed 
upper low will gradually shift southeast Thursday into Friday with a 
pair of shortwaves digging well into the Mid-Atlantic. As these 
shortwaves interact with the parent upper low, the associated long 
wave will become negatively tilted amplifying the flow pattern along 
the east coast. Current guidance shows a strengthening subtropical 
jet off the coast of the Mid-Atlantic, with an associated tight 
thermal gradient south and east of southern New England. As 
expected, models show 850-700mb frontogenesis maximized in this 
thermal gradient along and south of southern New England. These 
factors do not bode confidence in this system bringing large scale 
impacts to Vermont, but raw guidance including statistical and AI-
driven forecast suggest it is worth continuing to monitor. We 
recently highlighted preparedness for winter weather across New 
England, and so it is good to be ready whether or not something 
takes place. As of 2 PM on Monday, though, the GFS is the only model 
solution denoting an impactful system for Vermont and the north 
Country, with the Euro, CMC, and RRFS showing a more suppressed 
southerly system, keeping us on the northern periphery of the 
system. Regardless, temperatures by Friday will struggle to reach 40 
across the area as will sit in cold subsidence under the upper low. 

Perhaps more notable, regardless of how Thursday and Friday play 
out, will be the shift to northwest flow leading to some upslope 
snow showers Saturday and Sunday. There is higher confidence that 
regardless of the system track, that behind the upper low, winds 
will turn northwest, with cold advective upslope snow showers in the 
western facing slopes of the Greens and northern Adirondacks. 
Amounts will be uncertain due to differences in moisture profiles, 
but some wet snow in the mountains appears likely this weekend. NBM 
72 hour probabilities of 1 inch or more in the eastern Greens and 
Adirondacks through Sunday are around 40-50%.
